name: Strategies for Integrating AI into Your Organization
objectives: For a real or practice organization, score its AI readiness from 1 to 5 in leadership, people, data, processes and rules, with one sentence of evidence for each score and a fix for the two lowest
Given the organization's mission, write three SMART goals for AI that serve the mission, each with a number and a date
For the people who will use AI, write a one-page AI use policy, covering approved tools, what never goes in, human review, disclosure and a contact person
For each planned AI use, build a risk table using Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with likelihood, impact, a control and who checks it for every risk
For the team that will adopt AI, write a training and communication plan, that says why, what, and what is in it for them, and names at least one AI champion
Given your goals, policy, risks and training, create a 90-day roadmap in three phases, with an owner and a due date for every step

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Checking your organization's AI readiness
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Score an organization's readiness for AI in five areas.
This lesson builds toward: For a real or practice organization, you will score its AI readiness from 1 to 5 in leadership, people, data, processes and rules, with one sentence of evidence for each score and a fix for the two lowest.
Before buying tools, check readiness. Many AI efforts fail not because the tool is bad but because the people, data or rules were not ready.
Score five areas from 1 (not ready) to 5 (ready). Leadership: do leaders support it and set time aside? People: do staff, players or volunteers have basic digital skills? Data: is your information organized and stored safely? Processes: are your main tasks written down? Rules: do you have privacy and security rules?
Low scores are not a reason to stop. They tell you where to start. An athlete's business with great social media skills but messy records might start by organizing files before using AI on them.
Step by step:
- Score leadership, people, data, processes and rules from 1 to 5.
- Write one sentence of evidence for each score.
- Circle the two lowest scores.
- Note one fix for each low score.
Words to know:
- Readiness: how prepared an organization is to start something new.
- Data: the information an organization keeps, like schedules, records and files.
Try it now: Pick a real or practice organization. Score its readiness in the five areas with one sentence of evidence each, and name the first fix for the two lowest.
You can now score an organization's AI readiness and find where to start.

check.q: Which question checks the "processes" readiness area?
options: Are your main tasks written down?
check.why: Processes asks whether the main tasks are written down.

check.q: Your sports academy scores 2 on data and 5 on people. What do you do?
options: Buy the most advanced AI tool right away
Start by fixing the data area, such as organizing records
check.why: Low scores show where to start, not a reason to stop.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting AI goals tied to the mission
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write three measurable AI goals that serve the organization's mission.
This lesson builds toward: Given the organization's mission, you will write three SMART goals for AI that serve the mission, each with a number and a date.
AI should serve the mission, not the other way around. Start with what the organization exists to do: develop young athletes, grow a brand, serve meals, sell great products.
Then ask where AI could help that mission: more time with athletes or clients, faster replies to families or customers, better use of data, lower costs. Turn each into a measurable goal: "Cut weekly admin time for coaches from 6 hours to 3 by March."
Use the SMART check: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant to the mission and time-bound. Three goals are enough for 90 days.
Step by step:
- Write the mission in one sentence.
- List three ways AI could support it.
- Turn each into a SMART goal with a number and a date.
Words to know:
- Mission: the main purpose an organization exists for.
- SMART goal: a goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Try it now: Write the organization's mission in one sentence and three SMART AI goals that support it.
You can now set measurable AI goals that serve an organization's mission.

check.q: In SMART, what does the "R" mean?
check.why: A SMART goal is relevant to the organization's mission.

check.q: An athlete's brand wants to "use AI more". How do you make it a SMART goal?
options: "Reply to fan and sponsor emails within 24 hours, down from 3 days, by June."
check.why: It is specific, measurable, tied to the mission and has a date.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a one-page AI use policy
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a short AI use policy that tells people what is allowed, what is not and who to ask.
This lesson builds toward: For the people who will use AI, you will write a one-page AI use policy, covering approved tools, what never goes in, human review, disclosure and a contact person.
An AI use policy is a short set of rules for how people in the organization use AI. Without one, people guess, and someone may paste private player, client or donor information into a free tool.
Keep it to one page and cover: approved tools; what may never go into AI (health records, Social Security and bank numbers, private contracts, children's information, passwords); human review before anything AI-made is published or sent; honesty about AI use where it matters; and who to ask with questions.
Add special rules for your field. Sports organizations should protect athlete health and performance data and minors' information. Nonprofits should protect donor and client records. Get legal advice for contracts, endorsements and data laws that apply to you.
Step by step:
- List approved AI tools.
- List information that must never go into AI.
- Require a person to review AI output before it is sent or published.
- Say when AI use should be disclosed.
- Name a contact person for questions.
- Set a date to review the policy.
Words to know:
- Policy: a written rule everyone in an organization follows.
- Human review: a person checking AI output before it is used.
Try it now: Write a one-page AI use policy for your organization with all six parts. Ask an AI assistant to check it for anything unclear, then edit it yourself.
You can now write a short AI use policy that protects people and data.

check.q: Why does an organization need an AI use policy?
options: So people do not guess and paste private information into AI tools
check.why: Without a policy, people guess, and private player, client or donor data can leak.

check.q: A coach wants AI to draft a sponsorship contract. What should your policy say?
options: Send the AI draft to the sponsor right away
Get legal advice on contracts; a person reviews anything AI-made
Contracts are not covered by any rule
Paste the full private contract into a free AI tool
check.why: Contracts need legal advice, and AI output is reviewed by a person.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Managing AI risk with a simple framework
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a risk table for an AI use and assign a control to each risk.
This lesson builds toward: For each planned AI use, you will build a risk table using Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with likelihood, impact, a control and who checks it for every risk.
The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) publishes a free, voluntary AI Risk Management Framework. Its four core functions are Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. You can use them in plain language even in a small organization.
Govern: who is responsible and what the rules are (your policy). Map: for each AI use, what could go wrong and who could be hurt. Measure: how you will notice problems, such as spot-checking answers. Manage: what you do about each risk, such as human review or not using AI for that task.
Common AI risks: wrong facts, private data leaks, unfair treatment of people, copyright problems and damage to reputation. Write each in a risk table with how likely it is, how bad it would be, and the control.
Step by step:
- List each planned AI use.
- For each, write what could go wrong and who could be hurt.
- Rate likelihood and impact: low, medium or high.
- Add a control for each risk.
- Name who checks that the control works.
Words to know:
- NIST: the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, which publishes technical standards and guidance.
- Risk table: a list of risks with how likely and how serious each is, and what you will do about it.
Official sources:
- NIST AI Risk Management Framework
Try it now: Make a risk table for two AI uses in your plan, with at least three risks each, a likelihood and impact rating, a control and a person who checks it.
You can now map AI risks and assign controls using the four NIST functions.

check.q: In the NIST framework, which function is about what you do about each risk?
check.why: Manage is the action you take on each risk, such as human review.

check.q: AI will draft injury updates for parents. What control fits the risk of wrong facts?
options: A trainer or coach reviews every update before it is sent
check.why: Human review before sending controls the risk of wrong facts.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Leading people through the change
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a training and communication plan that helps people adopt AI.
This lesson builds toward: For the team that will adopt AI, you will write a training and communication plan, that says why, what, and what is in it for them, and names at least one AI champion.
People worry about AI: Will it replace me? Will I look foolish? Is it allowed? Ignoring those worries slows everything down. Address them openly.
Communicate the why (the mission and goals), the what (which tools and rules) and the what's in it for me (less admin, more time for coaching, clients or family). Name AI champions: one or two people who learn first and help others.
Train in small doses: a 30-minute hands-on session per tool, a one-page cheat sheet of good prompts, and a place to ask questions. Celebrate early wins in team meetings.
Step by step:
- Write a short message: why, what, and what is in it for them.
- Choose one or two AI champions.
- Plan 30-minute hands-on training sessions.
- Make a one-page prompt cheat sheet.
- Share early wins in meetings.
Words to know:
- Change management: helping people move from the old way of working to a new one.
- AI champion: a team member who learns first and helps others.
Try it now: Write a five-sentence announcement to your team, players, staff or volunteers about the AI plan, and a training schedule for the first month.
You can now plan training and communication that helps people adopt AI.

check.q: What is a prompt cheat sheet?
options: A one-page list of good prompts people can copy
A secret way around the policy
check.why: A one-page sheet of good prompts helps people get started fast.

check.q: Staff are nervous and avoiding the new AI tool. What do you do?
options: Force them to use it with no training
Wait for them to figure it out alone
Remove the tool without telling anyone
Address worries openly, run a short hands-on session and share early wins
check.why: Open talk, small hands-on training and early wins help people adopt AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building the 90-day roadmap
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn goals, policy, risks and training into a 90-day roadmap with owners and dates.
This lesson builds toward: Given your goals, policy, risks and training, you will create a 90-day roadmap in three phases, with an owner and a due date for every step.
A roadmap puts everything in order with dates. Split 90 days into three 30-day phases. Days 1-30: foundations (policy approved, files organized, champions trained). Days 31-60: pilots (one or two small AI uses tested with measures). Days 61-90: review and expand (decide what to keep, scale or stop).
Every step needs an owner and a due date. A step with no owner usually does not happen.
Plan a check-in every two weeks and a review at day 90 against your SMART goals. Then write the next 90-day plan. AI tools and rules change fast, so review the policy at least every six months.
Step by step:
- Days 1-30: foundations.
- Days 31-60: pilots with measures.
- Days 61-90: review, then expand or stop.
- Give every step an owner and date.
- Schedule check-ins every two weeks and a day-90 review.
Words to know:
- Roadmap: a plan that shows steps in order with dates.
- Owner: the person responsible for getting a step done.
Try it now: Final task: build your 90-day roadmap in a table with phase, step, owner and date, and attach your readiness score, goals, policy, risk table and training plan to complete your AI integration plan.
You can now write a complete 90-day plan to bring AI into an organization safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Readiness and goals No readiness score, or goals with no number or date. A readiness score in five areas and three SMART goals tied to the mission. Each goal links to a low readiness area it will fix or work around. AI use policy Missing what never goes into AI, or no human review. One page with approved tools, what never goes in, human review, disclosure and a contact person. Adds rules for the field, such as athlete health data and minors, and a review date. Risk table Risks listed with no controls. Each AI use has risks with likelihood, impact, a control and who checks. Covers wrong facts, data leaks and unfair treatment, and maps to Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Training and communication No plan for telling or training people. A message with why, what and what is in it for them, champions and short training sessions. Includes a prompt cheat sheet and a way to share early wins. 90-day roadmap Steps have no owners or dates. Three 30-day phases, each step with an owner and date, and check-ins every two weeks. Includes a day-90 review against the SMART goals and a policy review date. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What happens in days 61-90 of the roadmap?
options: Review the pilots and decide what to keep, scale or stop
check.why: The last phase reviews pilots and expands or stops them.

check.q: Your roadmap says "train staff" with no name or date. What do you add?
options: An owner and a due date
check.why: A step with no owner and date usually does not get done.
